cues.text: A Bleeding Host
In 1405, at Bois-Seigneur-Isaac in what is now Belgium, a consecrated Host bled during Mass, staining the corporal on which it lay.
As with many Eucharistic accounts from this period, the earliest surviving record of precisely what preceded the bleeding is thin.
However, the physical relic it produced — and the ecclesiastical response to it — is unusually well documented for an event of this age.
Episcopal Recognition
Rather than remain purely local, the event received formal diocesan attention within a few years.
On May 3, 1413, Peter d'Ailly, Bishop of Cambrai — the diocese then encompassing the region — formally authorized devotion to the miracle's relic.
He also authorized a solemn annual procession in its honor.
The first such procession took place the following year, in 1414.
A Monastery Built on the Site

The devotion continued to grow through the following decade, and on January 13, 1424, Pope Martin V granted approval for the construction of a monastery at Bois-Seigneur-Isaac itself, built specifically to house and honor the relic of the bleeding Host.

The choice to build directly on the site, rather than simply enshrine the relic elsewhere, reflects how quickly and how formally the event had been embraced by Church authority at both the diocesan and papal level.
A Living Pilgrimage Site

The monastery at Bois-Seigneur-Isaac remains an active goal of pilgrimage today, more than six centuries after the events of 1405, and the corporal stained with blood is still exposed for veneration in the chapel built to house it.

Few Eucharistic accounts of this early period carry as clear and continuous a paper trail of formal ecclesiastical approval — bishop, procession, and papal authorization for a monastery, each step documented and dated.
Legacy
What distinguishes Bois-Seigneur-Isaac among the many bleeding-Host accounts of the late medieval period is not the phenomenon itself.
That phenomenon recurs across dozens of similar traditions in this era.
Rather, it is the unusually swift and formal response of Church authority — a bishop's explicit authorization within eight years, papal approval for a monastery within nineteen.
That institutional care, more than any single miraculous detail, is what carried the devotion intact from a fifteenth-century Mass to the pilgrims who still visit the site today.
